newsitem.title: USA: Kidnapping is growth industry in Latin America.
newsitem.headline: Kidnapping is growth industry in Latin America.

text.p: Kidnapping is a growth industry in Latin America.
More people are abducted for ransom in the region than anywhere else in the world and the problem is worsening, particularly in Mexico, Colombia and Guatemala, according to a U.S. security expert.

The kidnappers' main target is rich nationals. While the threat to foreign executives and other expatriates is still low, it is increasing and U.S. business interests are at risk, said Bruce Groslin, director of Kroll Associates security and risk management consultants.
"It's a business. You're a commodity," he told a businessmen's forum on Wednesday in Miami, where many companies dealing in Latin America are based.
"They pride themselves on doing a good job because they want you to know they're serious."
Goslin said the world's highest ransoms are paid in Latin America, with most kidnappings carried out simply for money, not political reasons.

In some countries, the end of wars has led to a crime boom because of the numbers of unemployed former combatants and the plethora of guns. Gangs are often in league with corrupt police officers or soldiers, he added.
Colombia has the highest kidnapping rate in the world -- about 5,000 per year and rising. Guerrillas were responsible for about 50 percent and criminals the rest, a Kroll briefing said.
More expatriates are kidnapped in Colombia than in any other country and kidnappers will hold hostages for years.

In Mexico, there were about 1,400 ransom kidnappings in 1995 and the rate is increasing, the briefing said. The recent abduction of a Sanyo executive raised the risks for expatriates considerably, it said.
The links between police and drug traffickers along the U.S.-Mexican border made it a particularly dangerous area.
"Efforts to purge security force miscreants have increased the pool of trained criminals," it added.
Kidnapping in Brazil is a big problem for wealthy locals, with an estimated 800 cases last year. Police are often involved, particularly in Rio de Janeiro.
A kidnapping boom in Guatemala has coincided with a purge of corrupt military and police officers, and serious crime in tourist areas there is growing fast.

In El Salvador, the ranks of demobilized combatants after a long civil war and returned refugees, particularly from Los Angeles, are fuelling violent crimes. Personnel from multinational companies have been abducted in oil-producing areas of Ecuador, while in Panama gangs have targeted businesmen and the children of rich families.
Advising the businessmen on their own security, Goslin said most measures were common sense.
"Prepare beforehand, be alert, don't walk around strange cities after dark. Vary your routine."
People negotiating with kidnappers should not agree to a deal too fast or they might face another ransom demand. "It's called the double hit. They do it all the time," he said.

And if you become a kidnap victim, "the worst thing you can do is negotiate with the people who kidnap you. Co-operate with them but tell them as little as possible about yourself. Don't let them know anything about your financial position."
